# Suvaṇṇasāmajātaka (Ja 540)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Suvaṇṇasāmajātaka* (Ja 540, PTS Jātaka VI 68ff.), commonly known as the *Sāma-jātaka*, is one of the celebrated "last ten" great jātakas (*Mahānipāta*) [Appleton 2010; Collins 2016; Cabezon 2017]. In the Theravāda tradition, it is associated with the Bodhisatta's perfection of loving-kindness (*mettā-pāramī*) and the virtue of supporting one's parents [Appleton 2010; Hazra 1994]. The narrative frame (*paccuppannavatthu*) is set at Jetavana, where the Buddha recounts the story in response to a monk who was criticized by his peers for using alms to sustain his aged, destitute parents [SuttaCentral; Wilson, Buddhism and Family].
In the core narrative, two former deities of the Brahma-world marry without carnal desire and adopt the ascetic life, conceiving a son virginally without sexual intercourse [Collins, Nirvana and other Buddhist felicities; Cabezon 2017; Nyanaponika, Hecker, Bodhi 2003]. Their son Sāma (the Bodhisatta) dutifully provides for them after they are both blinded by snake venom [Appleton 2010; Walker, Unfolding Buddhism]. While drawing water at the river, Sāma is fatally wounded by a poisoned arrow and laments not his own death, but that he can no longer serve his blind parents [Walker, Unfolding Buddhism]. The story is also cited elsewhere in Pali literature, such as in the *Milindapañha* (Mil 5.4.6) [SuttaCentral].
The text has left a prominent imprint across Buddhist art, liturgy, and scholarship. Scenes from the jātaka appear on Sri Lankan festival gateways (*toraṇa*) and in eighteenth-century Mon murals in Thailand [Appleton 2010; Collins 2016]. In Cambodian chanted leporellos, vernacular verse compositions preserve the dramatic laments of both Sāma and his mother [Walker, Unfolding Buddhism]. In nineteenth-century scholarship, Eugène Burnouf prepared an extensive 449-page unpublished translation of a Burmese *nissaya* commentary on the text [Lopez 1995].
Curated passage-level parallels identified by SuttaCentral connect the text to the *Soṇanandajātaka* (Ja 532), the *Sattigumbajātaka* (Ja 503), and the *Vessantarajātaka* (Ja 547) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus confirms these shared verses, recording identical passages with Ja 532 (§46.4–49.4) and Ja 503 (§46.4–49.4), alongside 27 matching segments shared with Ja 547 and overlaps with the *Ummādantījātaka* (Ja 527), *Tesakuṇajātaka* (Ja 521), and the *Cariyāpiṭaka-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus]. Outside Pali, DharmaNexus automatically aligns the text with Sanskrit narratives in the *Mahāvastu-avadāna*, *Āryasaṃghāṭasūtra*, and *Dharmasamuccaya*, as well as Tibetan versions in the *Bodhisatvāvadānakalpalatā* and *Suvarṇavarṇāvadāna* [DharmaNexus].
